I am seventy years old, and I have farmed these fields in Quzhou County since I was a young man. I never went to school, but I know this land better than any book. I have six mu of good flat land on the North China Plain, and every year I do the same rotation: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is what our village has always done, and it is what puts food on the table.

The wheat went into the ground last October before the frost came. Now it is spring, and the wheat is waking up. I will give it one round of topdressing with urea when it greens up, and I will irrigate it three more times after the winter irrigation I already gave it — at jointing, at heading, and once more if the weather turns dry before harvest in early June. I use improved wheat seed, the kind they sell at the township supply store, and I rotary-till the soil before sowing. I put down about one hundred jin of compound fertilizer per mu at sowing time, and I topdress in spring. I spray for insects twice and for weeds once, because if you let the aphids or barnyard grass get ahead of you, the crop suffers.

After the wheat comes off in June, I plant hybrid maize the same day or the next — no time to waste, and I plant it no-tillage into the wheat stubble to keep the moisture in and save my old back from extra work. Hybrid maize grows fast and strong. I put down compound fertilizer in the rows at planting, and I irrigate twice: once when the seedlings need it, and once when the plants are tall and the ears are forming. I watch for corn borers and spray two or three times if I see damage, plus one herbicide spray.

I do not chase the highest yields anymore. At my age, I want steady, reliable harvests. I expect about one thousand jin of wheat per mu, and a bit more than that for maize. That gives us enough flour and enough grain to sell a little for cash. My children help me now with the heavy work, and we manage.
